nameStory: Meadow salsify gets one of its most charming names, "Jack-go-to-bed-at-noon," from its flower's peculiar habit of closing up by midday, as if it's ready for an afternoon nap! The name "goat's-beard" comes from its fluffy seed head that resembles the wispy whiskers of a billy goat. "Salsify" comes from an old French word meaning "satisfying," likely referring to its edible roots that were once commonly harvested.
description: Meadow salsify is a tall, slender wildflower that can reach 2-3 feet high, looking somewhat like a giant dandelion's sophisticated cousin. It produces bright yellow, daisy-like flowers that have the unusual habit of closing by noon each day, followed by spectacular puffy seed heads. This biennial plant (taking two years to complete its life cycle) has narrow, grass-like leaves and a thick taproot. The entire plant contains a milky white sap that oozes out when broken.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow composite flowers about 1-2 inches across that close by midday, opening again the next morning - this daily routine is the plant's signature behavior

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow, grass-like leaves that clasp the stem at their base and feel smooth to the touch with prominent parallel veins

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Large, spherical seed heads like oversized dandelion puffs, often 2-3 inches across, with feathery white bristles that feel soft and silky

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Thick, hollow stems that exude milky white latex when broken - this sap will stick to your fingers and has a slightly bitter smell

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall and upright with a single main stem that branches near the top, growing from a thick, carrot-like taproot

habitat: Look for meadow salsify in open fields, meadows, roadsides, and disturbed areas throughout New England's lower elevations. It thrives in well-drained soils and full sun, often appearing in the same grassy areas where you'd find dandelions and other common meadow flowers. This European native has naturalized widely and is particularly common in agricultural areas and along transportation corridors.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as rosettes of narrow leaves close to the ground, with the distinctive milky sap already present if leaves are broken.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time from June through August, when the characteristic yellow flowers open in morning and close by noon, followed by the showy seed heads.
seasonality.fall: Late flowers may persist into October, while mature seed heads continue dispersing their parachute-like seeds through early autumn.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely, leaving only the underground taproot to survive until the next growing season.

funFact: The root of meadow salsify tastes like oysters when cooked, earning it the nickname "vegetable oyster" among foragers - it was actually cultivated as a root vegetable in Europe and early America before being largely forgotten!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with yellow salsify (Tragopogon dubius), but yellow salsify has much larger flowers (2-3 inches across) and longer, pointed bracts that extend well beyond the flower petals like green rays. Remember: "dubius has dramatic bracts" while meadow salsify's bracts are shorter and less noticeable.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "salsify," this plant is not closely related to the true salsify (Scorzonera hispanica) commonly grown in vegetable gardens, though both have similar oyster-flavored roots. This naming confusion has led to mix-ups in foraging guides, so always double-check plant identification before harvesting.
compareHints: Meadow salsify differs from its cousin yellow salsify mainly in flower size and the bracts beneath the flower head - meadow salsify has smaller flowers and shorter bracts that don't extend past the petals. Both species have the same grass-like leaves and milky sap, but yellow salsify tends to grow taller and has an overall more robust appearance.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Yellow salsify is easily distinguished from its relative meadow salsify by its bright yellow flowers – meadow salsify has purple or violet blooms.
